Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A Saudi Arabian blogger detained in December, ostensibly because he supported reform advocates accused by the Saudi government of backing terrorism, has been released, a fellow blogger posted Saturday. Web sites like this one pushed for Fouad al-Farhan's release. Ahmed al-Omran said on his blog, saudijeans.org, and later told CNN that he was awakened by a text message from the wife of Fouad al-Farhan, saying he had been released and was at home with his family. "That's great news, and this is just how I wanted to start my morning," al-Omran wrote. He said he later spoke with al-Farhan for several minutes on the telephone. "He sounded fine; he seems to be in good spirits," al-Omran said. "He said he would have more to talk about later but not at this point. He said now he'd like to take some time to spend with his family, with his children that he hasn't seen for so long."  Watch al-Omran describe his conversation with al-Farhan » . A Web site set up to call for al-Farhan's release said, "Fouad is free. He is back home in Jeddah after 137 days in custody." The Saudi Interior Ministry said it had no immediate comment on the reports. In January, a ministry spokesman said al-Farhan was arrested December 10 "because he violated the regulations of the kingdom." But in an e-mail posted on al-Farhan's Web site after his arrest, he told friends that he faced arrest for supporting 10 reform advocates the Saudi government accused of backing terrorism. In the e-mail, al-Farhan said a senior Interior Ministry official promised that he would remain in custody for three days at most if he agreed to sign a letter of apology. "I'm not sure if I'm ready to do that," he wrote. "An apology for what? Apologizing because I said the government is [a] liar when they accused those guys of supporting terrorism?" Al-Farhan, who blogs at alfarhan.org, is one of the few Saudi Web commentators to use his own name, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. In January, the Bush administration expressed its concerns to the Saudi government regarding al-Farhan's detention at "a relatively senior level," U.S. State Department spokesman Sean McCormack said. "The U.S. stands for freedom of expression," McCormack said at the time. "Wherever people are seeking to express themselves, via the Internet or via other areas, whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere in the world, we stand with that freedom of expression, and that was our message to the Saudi government." The American Islamic Congress, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization, launched an online letter-writing campaign aimed at freeing al-Farhan, whom it called "the godfather of Saudi blogging." "All he did was express his opinions in a very obvious way, and he didn't threaten anyone," al-Omran said. "He was advocating against violence and terrorism." Al-Omran said al-Farhan had stopped blogging for a few months in late 2006, after the Interior Ministry ordered him to take down a blog he was operating, but he began again at a new site. He said al-Farhan told him he was treated well in jail. He also called al-Farhan's release a turning point for the blogging community in Saudi Arabia. "It showed the community of bloggers in Saudi Arabia can come together and support this cause -- support his freedom of speech -- even those who didn't agree with some of the things he wrote," he said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Mohammed Jamjoom contributed to this report.

# Saudi Blogger Freed After 137 Days in Detention

Fouad al-Farhan, one of Saudi Arabia's most prominent bloggers, has been released from custody after spending 137 days behind bars, ending a lengthy detention that drew international attention to the risks faced by online activists in the kingdom.

Al-Farhan was first detained in December after he published a blog post publicly criticizing the Saudi government's decision to accuse ten reform advocates of supporting terrorism. His outspoken commentary, which questioned the fairness and motives behind the accusations, appears to have prompted his arrest, though authorities never provided a clear legal justification. When pressed for details, Saudi officials offered only vague explanations, stating that al-Farhan had committed unspecified "violations of the kingdom's regulations." No formal charges were ever publicly disclosed, and he was held without trial for more than four months.

His detention quickly became a rallying point for bloggers, human rights advocates, and online activists both inside and outside Saudi Arabia. Many viewed his arrest as a clear example of the government's efforts to silence dissenting voices, particularly those using the internet to discuss politically sensitive topics such as reform, corruption, and human rights. Al-Farhan, who had built a reputation as one of the most widely read Arabic-language bloggers in the region, was seen by many as a symbol of the broader struggle for free expression in Saudi Arabia.

Throughout his time in custody, supporters organized online campaigns calling for his release, using blogs, forums, and social media to raise awareness of his case and pressure Saudi authorities. Fellow bloggers wrote extensively about the injustice of his detention, and the case drew attention from international press freedom organizations concerned about the treatment of internet commentators in the kingdom.

After 137 days, al-Farhan was finally released and reunited with his family, a moment that was met with widespread celebration among the online community that had campaigned tirelessly on his behalf. Bloggers across the region expressed relief and joy at the news, with many hailing it as a small but significant victory for freedom of expression.

Despite his release, al-Farhan's case remains a stark reminder of the precarious position occupied by bloggers and online commentators in Saudi Arabia, where criticism of the government—even when framed as a call for reform—can result in prolonged detention without formal charges. His ordeal has reinforced concerns among activists that the kingdom continues to use vague legal language and administrative detention as tools to suppress dissent, leaving little clarity or protection for those who speak out online.

The network has also reported on diplomatic developments between Saudi Arabia and Western nations, including shifting relationships with the United States under various presidential administrations.

CNN's journalism has often highlighted human rights concerns in Saudi Arabia, including the 2018 killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, which drew significant international attention and scrutiny of the kingdom's practices. As Saudi Arabia has sought to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy, CNN Business has covered major initiatives like NEOM, the futuristic city project, along with the kingdom's growing sovereign wealth fund investments across global markets, sports, and technology sectors.

CNN's coverage reflects the broader international media's challenge of balancing reporting on Saudi Arabia's modernization efforts with continued scrutiny of governance and human rights issues, presenting a multifaceted picture of a nation in transition.
